title: Generative large language models in the clinical management of Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment
container-title: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

custom.summary: Across 11 studies of large language models in Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment, the authors found the models rated best when writing educational material and answering caregiver questions, and weakest at diagnosis and treatment advice. Eight studies covered patient and caregiver education. Answers were mostly accurate: one study found 93% of answers to 60 caregiver forum posts correct, with none harmful. But every study that measured reading level found it above a sixth-grade level, and the answers cited no sources. Only two studies counted made-up content, and none tested the models in real care, so the authors advise that a clinician check the output.
custom.studied: published studies evaluating large language models for Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment care

title: Assessing the Quality of ChatGPT Responses to Dementia Caregivers' Questions: Qualitative Analysis

custom.summary: Three dementia clinicians judged most of ChatGPT-3.5's answers to 60 Reddit posts by dementia caregivers to be of high quality. Of the answers, 43% earned the full 5 points, 35% earned 4 and 22% earned 3, and none were judged harmful or made up. The posts dealt with memory loss and confusion, aggression, and driving. Each answer earned a point for being factual, reading the caregiver's need correctly, offering steps the caregiver could take, pulling ideas together, and being complete. The authors report weaker results on completeness, with 37% leaving out something clinicians thought mattered. Reading the situation was also weaker: 22% suggested things already tried or missed details, such as a person already in hospital.
custom.studied: questions posted by dementia caregivers on Reddit, answered by ChatGPT-3.5

title: Positive Design Framework for Carer eSupport: Qualitative Study to Support Informal Caregivers of Patients With Head and Neck Cancer in Sweden

custom.summary: In online focus groups with 15 Swedish family caregivers of people with head and neck cancer and 13 health care professionals, a chatbot was the least wanted feature for a planned web support service called Carer eSupport. Participants cited missing human contact, doubts about whether its answers could be trusted, little understanding of how chatbots work, and generic replies. Some would accept one for simple, non-urgent questions such as nutrition tips if staff answered the medical ones. Caregivers wanted tailored, plainly worded information, a staff-moderated forum and video meetings, and the authors built these into a design framework aimed at caregiver well-being.
custom.studied: Swedish family caregivers of people with head and neck cancer, and health care professionals

title: A Qualitative Study with Informal Caregivers and Healthcare Professionals for Individuals with Head and Neck Cancer on the Usage of AI Chatbots
container-title: Studies in health technology and informatics

custom.summary: Both family caregivers and clinicians in this Swedish study were largely reluctant to use AI chatbots in caring for people with head and neck cancer. The authors ran six focus groups with 15 informal caregivers (spouses, relatives or friends) and 13 healthcare professionals from three university hospitals. Participants doubted that chatbot information could be trusted, recalled poor earlier encounters with chatbots, and missed the human contact of talking with a person. The authors argue that future chatbots should be designed with their intended users involved throughout.
custom.studied: Informal caregivers and healthcare professionals of people with head and neck cancer at three Swedish university hospitals

title: A Personalized Chatbot to Support Kidney Disease Patients in Saudi Arabia: A Preliminary Study
container-title: Studies in health technology and informatics

custom.summary: The survey found that 95.5% of respondents in Saudi Arabia said they would be willing to use a chatbot (a program that answers questions in conversation) for help with chronic kidney disease. Respondents most wanted advice on diet, information about the illness, and emotional support. The authors ran an online questionnaire at a single point in time, aimed at patients and the people caring for them, and report that a chatbot could help with gaps in knowledge, the cost of treatment and managing diet. They plan to use the results to design a first version of such a chatbot.
custom.studied: kidney disease patients and caregivers in Saudi Arabia answering an online questionnaire

title: Assessing the Accuracy of ChatGPT in Answering Questions About Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness

custom.summary: Both ChatGPT 4o and ChatGPT o1 gave mostly accurate answers to 57 questions about prolonged disorders of consciousness (long-lasting loss of awareness after severe brain injury), each worded as a patient's relative might ask, in English and Italian. Expert raters judged 82.5% of o1's English answers fully correct, against 64.9% of 4o's Italian answers. Only two of 228 answers, both from 4o and about diagnostic tests, were judged misleading. Italian answers scored somewhat lower, significantly so only for 4o on clinical questions. 4o more often voiced sympathy, while o1 more often advised seeing a clinician in Italian.
custom.studied: ChatGPT answers to relative-style questions about prolonged disorders of consciousness, in English and Italian

title: Cultural and Linguistic Adaptation of the iSupport for Dementia Program: Perspectives From Vietnamese Carers in Australia

custom.summary: Vietnamese carers in Australia asked that the Vietnamese version of the WHO's iSupport for Dementia online training use natural translation, familiar examples and videos with real actors and voice-over, especially for people who read less easily. The authors held five focus groups in Vietnamese with 30 people (18 family carers and 12 formal carers) to judge the adapted program and to inform a planned virtual assistant version (iSupport VA). Participants valued the caregiving skills it teaches. They named lack of time, other duties and limited comfort with digital tools as obstacles, and asked for introductory tutorials and contact with other carers.
custom.studied: Vietnamese family and formal carers of people with dementia in Australia

title: Readability and Linguistic Characteristics of Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias Prevention, Symptom, and Treatment Information from Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots

custom.summary: The authors report that dementia information from free generative AI chatbots read at about a college level, harder than the level advised for patient handouts, and that answers about treatment were the hardest to read. They scored 66 chatbot answers on prevention, symptoms and treatment of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. They used standard readability formulas and a word-counting program that rates writing style and tone. The answers scored high for logical, analytical style but low for confidence, authenticity and positive tone. The authors advise dementia caregivers to keep these traits in mind when using chatbots for information.
custom.studied: answers from free generative AI chatbots about dementia prevention, symptoms and treatment

title: AgenticAD: A Specialized Multiagent System Framework for Holistic Alzheimer Disease Management

custom.summary: The authors built eight AI agents for Alzheimer's care, powered by large language models such as GPT-4o and Gemini, and report that each produced usable output in small demonstration runs, with some failures traced to outside tools. Caregiver-facing agents drafted personalized care plans from a form filled in as a family caregiver, clinician or person with memory concerns, wrote reports of over 1,000 words on three caregiver topics such as sundowning, and answered questions about uploaded PDFs. Other agents searched the web, scraped pages, queried datasets and described brain scans. No caregivers tried the system, and the authors judged the outputs themselves without formal scoring.
custom.studied: a multi-agent large language model system for Alzheimer's care, tested by its authors with example inputs

title: Acceptability and Usability of a Socially Assistive Robot Integrated With a Large Language Model for Enhanced Human-Robot Interaction in a Geriatric Care Institution: Mixed Methods Evaluation

custom.summary: Ratings of a talking robot in a Paris geriatric day hospital rose over three rounds of testing as its dialogue system moved from a rule-based design to an offline large language model (Vicuna-13B). Acceptability rose from 15.4 to 22.5 out of 30, and usability from 47.9 to 69.3 out of 100. The 97 participants were older patients and the family members or friends accompanying them. Each talked once with the ARI robot, which offered greetings, directions and hospital information, then rated it and explained their scores. The authors found no difference between patients' and caregivers' ratings. Final scores still fell below product-readiness thresholds, and users complained of off-topic replies and of being unable to interrupt the robot.
custom.studied: older outpatients and their accompanying family caregivers at a French geriatric day hospital

title: Designing a Multimodal and Culturally Relevant Alzheimer Disease and Related Dementia Generative Artificial Intelligence Tool for Black American Informal Caregivers: Cognitive Walk-Through Usability Study

custom.summary: In think-aloud testing with 15 Black American caregivers of people with dementia, participants wanted to hear answers read aloud while also reading them, asked for plainer wording and for information tailored to their community and local area, and suggested promoting the tool through town halls, churches and word of mouth. The authors built Lola, a phone app that uses ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo to answer dementia questions by typed text or by voice, drawing on Alzheimer's Association material. Each caregiver was over 50, and 12 of the 15 were 65 or older. Each completed three search tasks in a session of about 30 minutes, followed by questions about the app.
custom.studied: Black American family caregivers of people with dementia in the US Midwest testing a generative AI app

title: Navigating Life After Dementia Diagnosis: Questions, Challenges, and Support Needs Among Dementia Dyads
container-title: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences

custom.summary: Families early in mild cognitive impairment or dementia reported needing continuing, tailored help well after diagnosis, according to interviews meant to shape an AI chatbot for them. The authors interviewed 11 pairs of a person with the condition and their family care partner, one more care partner and 12 dementia care professionals in the US. Common questions covered everyday care, medical worries, changes in behaviour, what to expect, safety and where to find services. Reported obstacles included exhausted care partners, little knowledge of the disease, trouble finding their way through the health system, money and difficulty with technology.
custom.studied: US people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia, their family care partners, and dementia care professionals

title: Online health information-seeking behavior during the preoperative period among patients with pancreatic tumors and caregivers in China: A qualitative study

custom.summary: In interviews with 8 patients awaiting pancreatic tumor surgery and 12 unpaid family caregivers in Shanghai, half of participants (5 patients and 5 caregivers) said they had used a large language model such as DeepSeek before the operation, mostly to read test reports. Users described the answers as vague and lacking firm conclusions, and they noticed that rewording a question changed the reply. Most treated clinicians as the final word, though one patient trusted the AI fully. The authors report that caregivers, often adult children, led searches across social media, AI and medical platforms, and that participants wanted hospital-backed, plain-language guidance, with AI handling simple questions and staff handling complex ones.
custom.studied: patients awaiting pancreatic tumor surgery and their unpaid family caregivers at a Shanghai cancer center

title: Shaping the Future of Caregiving Technology: Caregiver Tech Insights Survey, Findings Report 2026

custom.summary: Of 272 family caregivers who answered Caregiver Action Network's 2026 email survey, 59% said they had used AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini for caregiving: 33% regularly and 26% once or twice. The most common uses were making sense of a diagnosis (44%), preparing questions for doctor visits (32%), organizing medical information (27%) and emotional support (24%). The survey also found that 37% spend 11 or more hours a week coordinating care. The leading barriers to adopting technology were cost (43%), not knowing which products to trust (42%) and privacy worries (40%).
custom.studied: family caregivers on Caregiver Action Network's email list

title: Assessing the accuracy and reliability of ChatGPT's medical responses about thyroid cancer

custom.summary: The authors report that ChatGPT answered 23 of 30 general thyroid cancer questions correctly (76.66%), and 2 answers (6.66%) mixed correct facts with wrong or outdated ones. Its advice on three patient cases was judged inadequate, because the treatment and follow-up guidance it gave was generic and did not address each specific patient. When asked about emotional support, it gave patients and their families practical advice on next steps and on coming to terms with a new diagnosis. Three endocrinologists (hormone and gland specialists) graded the answers against the American Thyroid Association's guidelines.
custom.studied: ChatGPT's answers to thyroid cancer questions, patient cases and emotional-support prompts

title: Conversational AI in Cognitive and Social Training for People with Dementia: A Systematic Review

custom.summary: The review found that the firmest controlled evidence came from low-cost tools such as text chatbots, phone services and web apps: a 43-country trial of the PDC30 caregiver chatbot (274 caregivers) reported less depression and burden after one month. The authors pooled 40 studies from 2015 to 2026 on conversational AI for people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment and their caregivers. Of these, 24 used social robots, 12 used text chatbots, and only 8 were randomized trials. Eight used large language models, which lengthened conversations and were preferred by caregivers, but none had been tested against usual care in a large trial. Speech recognition failures were the most common technical problem.
custom.studied: studies of conversational AI, including social robots and chatbots, for people with dementia or MCI and their caregivers

title: Automated Benchmark Generation from Domain Guidelines Informed by Bloom's Taxonomy

custom.summary: The authors built a method that turns expert guidance into test questions for language models. They report that eight models averaged between about 68% and 77% correct on a caregiving set drawn from a stroke recovery guide, which proved easier than their teaching and diet sets. From 52 caregiving practices they generated 5,000 scenarios, 20,000 multiple-choice questions at four levels of Bloom's Taxonomy (a scale running from simple recall to analysis), and 5,000 practice dialogues. Models often did better on analysis questions than on recall. Training smaller models on the dialogues gave modest gains on the caregiving questions.
custom.studied: synthetic caregiving scenarios, questions and dialogues built from a stroke recovery guide

title: Moral Advice as Interactional Negotiation: Framing, User Pressure, and Social Position in Large Language Model Responses

custom.summary: When a simulated adult child said they had cared for their parents, GPT-4o-mini approved every time, yet after one reply of disagreement it switched its view in 90.1% of persona setups. When the user said they had not provided care, the model mostly disapproved and gave way later, less often, or unpredictably. The authors ran a three-round test in Chinese across 810 persona profiles that varied gender, age, region, education and siblings, for 4,860 conversations in all. Female personas and those with a sister were more readily excused from caregiving. Repeating identical runs gave the same pattern in only 14% of the non-caregiving setups.
custom.studied: GPT-4o-mini's advice to simulated adult children about caring for elderly parents

title: The PDC30 Chatbot-Development of a Psychoeducational Resource on Dementia Caregiving Among Family Caregivers: Mixed Methods Acceptability Study

custom.summary: The authors report that 21 Hong Kong family caregivers of relatives with dementia rated the PDC30 Chatbot favourably after two weeks of use: 15 (71%) used it more than once a day and 16 (76%) said they would recommend it. The chatbot runs on GPT-4o and draws its answers only from a self-help caregiving guidebook. On 21 typical caregiver questions, the authors judged it and a second chatbot built on charity and government pages to give more focused advice than ChatGPT, with PDC30 offering more coping ideas for emotional questions. Written comments centred on helpfulness, round-the-clock access, and doubts about AI that eased with use.
custom.studied: Hong Kong family caregivers of relatives with dementia, recruited through a university campus

title: Intervention Without Borders - an Automated Self-Guided AI-Enhanced Psychoeducation Intervention for Dementia Caregivers: Parallel-Group Randomized Waitlist-Controlled Trial
container-title: The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry

custom.summary: The authors report that dementia caregivers using PDC30, an automated online program built around an AI counselling chatbot, had less depression and burden after one month than those still waiting for it. The trial randomised 274 caregivers from 43 countries, each giving 10 or more hours of care a week and showing at least mild depressive symptoms. One-month gains were modest to moderate (standardised effect sizes of about 0.34 to 0.42), and anxiety did not improve. Once the waitlist group got access, the two groups looked alike, and gains held to three months. Users said they visited several times a week and rated the chatbot the most helpful part.
custom.studied: family caregivers of relatives with dementia living in the community, recruited online from 43 countries

title: Multiple Therapeutic Mechanisms of an Automated Self-Guided AI-Enhanced Psychoeducation Intervention for Dementia Family Caregivers: Randomized Waitlist-Controlled Trial
container-title: The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry

custom.summary: The authors report that the benefits of PDC30, a self-guided online program for family caregivers of people with dementia that includes an AI counseling chatbot among its tools, worked mainly through two changes: caregivers' confidence in controlling upsetting thoughts, and their use of positive reappraisal (finding a more helpful way to see a hard situation). The trial randomly assigned 274 caregivers from 43 countries to the program or to a one-month waitlist. Lower depression, lower burden and a greater sense of gain were each linked to these changes. Confidence in handling a relative's difficult behaviors also explained part of the drop in burden.
custom.studied: family caregivers of relatives with dementia, with at least mild depressive symptoms, in 43 countries

title: Optimizing ChatGPT's Interpretation and Reporting of Delirium Assessment Outcomes: Exploratory Study

custom.summary: The authors report that ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4, after being fed the published validation paper for the Sour Seven, scored five standard hospital case stories much as five human experts did. The Sour Seven is a seven-item delirium checklist designed for family members and untrained nurses. Both models flagged delirium in the four cases that showed it and not in the dementia-only case. Before prompts were refined, ChatGPT-3.5 sometimes applied the wrong score cut-offs and ChatGPT-4 gave half scores the checklist does not allow. Stricter prompts that asked for a table and limited advice to the form's two follow-up steps fixed most errors, and ChatGPT-4 varied less across its 25 runs.
custom.studied: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 applying an informant-based delirium checklist to standard clinical case vignettes, compared with five expert raters

title: A Goal-Oriented Chatbot for Engaging the Elderly Through Family Photo Conversations

custom.summary: The authors built a GPT-4 chatbot that talks with older adults about family photos, and report that in simulated chats it kept a structured flow while letting the user drift off topic, though it sometimes misjudged whether a reply had answered its question. It asks who, where, when and what about each photo, gently corrects wrong answers, then invites open reminiscence. After each chat it updates a list of the person's likes and dislikes and suggests the next photo. Caregivers use a web portal to upload photos and descriptions and to read chat summaries. Testing used a second language model playing an older man, and no real older adults or caregivers took part.
custom.studied: a photo-based reminiscence chatbot for older adults with a caregiver web portal, tested against a simulated elderly user

title: How people use Copilot for Health

custom.summary: Microsoft AI researchers report that about one in seven Copilot conversations about symptoms or medical conditions concerned another person, such as a child, an aging parent or a partner. They sorted a random sample of more than 500,000 health conversations from January 2026 into 12 kinds of request, using a language model checked against clinician labels. Roughly one in five conversations dealt with the user's own symptoms or conditions, and general health information made up over 40%. Questions about symptoms and emotional health rose in the evening and at night, phones carried more personal questions than desktops, and many requests were about finding providers or understanding insurance.
custom.studied: de-identified consumer health conversations with Microsoft Copilot

title: Talk with Ted: An embodied conversational agent for caregivers

custom.summary: Caregivers who trained by talking with Ted, an animated on-screen character that holds spoken conversations, reported feeling emotionally attached to it and still remembered its lessons eight weeks later, according to the authors. Ted was built to teach caregivers how to communicate well with people living with dementia, many of whom struggle to express their needs. The team compared it with an online course across 23 caregivers (12 used Ted, 11 the course) over eight weeks, using both measures and interviews. Caregivers said they applied what they learned in their care, and the authors report that people with dementia responded well to the changes.
custom.studied: caregivers of people living with dementia trained with an embodied conversational agent or an online course

title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Applications in Dementia Caregiving: A Scoping Review of Technologies, Functions, and Evidence Gaps

custom.summary: The authors found 43 studies of AI built to help people caring for someone with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. The tools fell into three groups: physical robots, conversational agents such as chatbots, and predictive algorithms. According to the review, these tools helped caregivers by teaching them about the condition, assisting with everyday tasks, offering social support and helping manage clinical care. The authors searched two databases, CINAHL and PubMed, and call for more rigorous studies that follow these tools over longer periods.
custom.studied: published studies of AI tools for caregivers of people with dementia

title: Patient- and Caregiver-Informed Considerations for the Design and Implementation of Generative AI-Supported Patient-Centered Clinical Decision Support: Qualitative Study

custom.summary: Patient and caregiver advocates in this qualitative study wanted generative AI tools for health decisions to come with clear rules on data use and security, to be designed and tested with patients, caregivers and clinicians, and to support clinicians without replacing them. The authors ran six virtual small-group discussions with 16 advocates (10 patient, 5 caregiver, 1 both), built around two example tools: a patient portal assistant that asks follow-up questions about symptoms, and a text-message medication check-in. In the second phase, 8 of 9 participants rated transparency and security standards extremely important. Participants thought such tools could help caregivers with routine tasks like medication reminders.
custom.studied: patient and caregiver advocates discussing generative AI tools for patient-centered decision support

title: A single-blind, parallel-group randomised trial of a Technology-assisted and remotely delivered Cognitive Behavioural Therapy intervention (Tech-CBT) versus usual care to reduce anxiety in people with mild cognitive impairment and dementia: study protocol for a randomised trial

custom.summary: This protocol sets out a planned Australian trial and reports no results yet. The authors plan to enrol 70 people with mild cognitive impairment or dementia who have anxiety. Each will be randomly assigned either to usual care or to six weekly video sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy, a talking therapy that teaches coping skills, adapted here to focus on relaxation. Participants receive a tablet or an Amazon Echo smart speaker to join sessions, play relaxation media and keep logs by voice or screen. Family care partners, where available, are asked to join sessions and home practice. Their burden, mood and quality of life are secondary outcomes, alongside cost-effectiveness and usability interviews.
custom.studied: Australians with mild cognitive impairment or dementia and anxiety, and their family care partners where available

sample.of: people with MCI or dementia (planned enrolment)

title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients

custom.summary: The authors report that language models changed their mental health treatment advice depending on whether a clinician, a family caregiver or the person themselves described the same case. Across 35,055 answers from 41 models to 19 written cases, models urged seeing a professional in 95% of caregiver and patient answers compared with 66% for clinicians. Clinicians got doses and sequencing, while lay askers got hedged advice and more brand-name drugs. Asked an open question, models raised lisdexamfetamine for binge eating in 92% of clinician answers, 36% of caregiver answers and 18% of patient answers. In a separate scoring task, models mostly rated highly the options they recommended.
custom.studied: 41 language models answering mental health cases written as a clinician, a family caregiver or the patient

title: All four leading LLMs talk more than they listen to personality-verified synthetic help-seekers

custom.summary: In simulated chats with a synthetic family caregiver who had just learned that a relative has dementia, all four language models tested (GPT-4.1, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Mistral-Medium, DeepSeek-V3.2) wrote more words than the caregiver, at ratios of 1.8 to 3.3, and nearly nine in ten replies ran past 160 words. The models also tended to offer solutions before exploring the situation. The authors gave seven synthetic caregivers set personality, coping and resilience profiles, and a separate model rated 28 conversations. Rated stress and mood eased with every model and did not differ between them. Conduct did differ: DeepSeek-V3.2 scored highest overall and Mistral-Medium lowest.
custom.studied: four LLMs advising synthetic dementia caregivers in acute crisis after a relative's diagnosis

title: "It Felt Like I Was Left in the Dark": Exploring Information Needs and Design Opportunities for Family Caregivers of Older Adult Patients in Critical Care Settings

custom.summary: In this preprint, caregivers who tried a prototype said plain-language explanations and a day-by-day timeline helped them follow an older relative's intensive care stay, though several said they would still check chatbot answers with a doctor. The authors first interviewed 15 US family caregivers, who described scattered updates from busy staff, confusing lab reports and unproductive conversations with clinicians. They then built CareMap, which turns health record data into a visual timeline and a chatbot built on a large language model that explains results, answers questions and suggests questions to ask clinicians. Ten of the caregivers and 2 physicians tested it with synthetic patient data.
custom.studied: US family caregivers of older adults admitted to intensive care

title: Scoping review of AI-chatbots to support family caregivers

custom.summary: The authors found that research on chatbots for family caregivers is still young: of 505 records screened, 30 articles qualified, and none was a randomized trial. Seventeen tested existing tools, mostly ChatGPT, on caregiving questions; nine described newly built chatbots; four were commentaries, reviews or interview studies. Most dealt with dementia or cancer care and centred on giving information, with emotional support and pointers to local services less common. Experts usually rated answers for accuracy and readability, and caregivers themselves rarely judged them. The review reports mostly accurate, readable information, with thin and mixed evidence on emotional support and safety.
custom.studied: published articles on chatbots used in family caregiving, searched in four databases in early 2025

title: An Interactive LLM-Based Simulator for Dementia-Related Activities of Daily Living

custom.summary: Dementia-care experts rated an AI-simulated person with Alzheimer's as fairly believable during everyday care tasks, though the simulation often lost track of task steps and the care setting. The authors built a web tool in which gpt-5-mini plays a person at an early, middle or late stage during tasks such as taking medicines, while the user replies as the caregiver in their own words or by picking one of four suggested communication approaches. Across 18 sessions with 14 experts (112 rated turns), average realism sat around 3.5 to 4 out of 5. Experts wrote their own replies in 54.5% of turns, and their comments most often flagged errors in following the steps of the task (9 of 20 commented turns).
custom.studied: an LLM simulator of a person with Alzheimer's during daily care tasks, tested by dementia-care experts

title: AI Companions for Young Adult Caregivers: Practical Advice, Emotional Depth, and the Limits of Metric Evaluation

custom.summary: In a user study with 90 young people who help care for someone, those who chatted with Carebot, a fine-tuned version of the open Gemma 3 27B model, were nearly four times as likely to call its replies too practical (49% against 13%). Overall ratings matched the unmodified model (about 7.4 of 10 for both). The authors trained Carebot on 10,000 synthetic caregiver conversations and chose it after expert reviewers preferred it to versions that look up documents (retrieval). An AI judge favoured it over the base model in 85% of comparisons. The authors argue that automated scores and expert review missed what young caregivers often wanted: to feel heard.
custom.studied: young adult caregivers in India using a fine-tuned AI companion or its base model

title: A Co-Designed and Bilingual WhatsApp-Based Chatbot Intervention (PflegeBot) for Informal Caregivers in Germany: Single-Arm Nonrandomized Feasibility Study

custom.summary: Caregivers who completed follow-up rated PflegeBot, a scripted WhatsApp chatbot in German or Turkish, as easy to use, with a mean of 82 out of 100 on a standard usability questionnaire; 76% of 46 scored at least 68, a common bar for acceptable usability. Of 102 adults caring for another adult who enrolled, 70 started the 12-week daily-message program and 49 returned any follow-up data. Only 1 of 45 respondents reported using its question-lookup feature. Stress, depression and loneliness scores fell slightly while burden rose, but the authors report that none of these changes was clearly different from zero.
custom.studied: German- and Turkish-speaking family caregivers of adults in Germany

title: When AI Says "I have been in similar situations": Synthetic Lived Experience in Peer-Like Caregiver Support

custom.summary: Human replies on two dementia caregiver forums drew on the writers' own caregiving stories far more than replies from three AI models told to answer like a peer, the authors report. Coding 1,000 forum replies, they found seven kinds of personal story, most often about navigating care systems (26%) and grief (19%). In 637 coded AI replies from LLaMA, GPT-4o-mini and MedGemma, the models usually offered emotional reassurance but turned lived detail into general advice, and LLaMA sometimes claimed caregiving experience it cannot have. The authors propose design limits, such as never implying personal experience and pointing caregivers to human peers when lived experience matters most.
custom.studied: caregiver posts and peer replies from r/Alzheimers and ALZConnected, and peer-prompted replies to those posts from three large language models

title: Inform, Coach, Relate, Listen: Auditing LLM Caregiving Support Roles

custom.summary: The authors report that the support role a language model is told to play changes how often its replies to dementia caregivers show risky patterns, such as overlooking part of the question or sounding overconfident. They answered 5,000 caregiver posts from Reddit and ALZConnected with three models under four roles (Inform, Coach, Relate, Listen) and two baselines. An AI judge then scored the 90,000 replies against a risk checklist built with clinicians. Among 125 online raters, Coach and Inform replies scored highest overall (3.81 and 3.79 of 5) and Listen lowest (3.10), even though the authors flag the more directive roles as riskier.
custom.studied: questions posted by dementia caregivers on Reddit r/Alzheimers and ALZConnected, answered by three language models

title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions

custom.summary: The authors report that feeding six large language models structured feedback from a caregiving risk rubric cut flagged problems in their answers by roughly 35% to 98% after one revision, and a second revision added little. The rubric, called RubRIX, was built from dementia caregivers' Reddit posts with clinician input. It scores 29 yes-or-no checks across five risks: ignoring distress, stigma, wrong information, agreeing with harmful beliefs, and overconfidence. An AI judge applied it to answers for 20,338 caregiver posts from ALZConnected and Reddit and matched human reviewers about 89% of the time. Clinicians found the revised answers gentler and more careful, though some errors stayed or were newly introduced.
custom.studied: LLM answers to posts by dementia and general caregivers on ALZConnected and Reddit

title: Stakeholder perspectives on artificial intelligence in schizophrenia care

custom.summary: Across focus groups at a New York City academic health center, participants described AI chatbots as a possible source of help between clinic visits, but named trust as the main obstacle, driven by privacy worries and risks particular to schizophrenia. The 28 participants (17 people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, 7 caregivers and 4 clinicians) discussed a hypothetical AI companion tool. The authors report five themes: round-the-clock availability, unclear purpose, doubts about trust, acceptance only as an add-on to human care, and a preference for limiting it to low-risk supportive uses. They conclude that any such tool should be open about how it works and have clear limits.
custom.studied: people with schizophrenia, their caregivers and clinicians at a New York City academic health center

title: Exploring evaluation measures of large language models for family caregiver use: A scoping review

custom.summary: Across 10 studies published up to July 2024, all of which tested ChatGPT, researchers judged chatbot answers for family caregivers mainly on four qualities: accuracy, reliability (getting the same answer twice), readability and comprehensiveness. The authors report accuracy of roughly 70% to 99%. Models still made mistakes on clinical cutoffs and treatment, and readability findings conflicted depending on the scoring method. A quicker update search through November 2025 found 14 more studies, still mostly about ChatGPT. The authors suggest caregivers use these tools for general learning and emotional support, check answers against a second model and a clinician, and avoid relying on them for medication or urgent decisions.
custom.studied: published studies evaluating large language model answers or materials for family caregivers

title: Automating collateral histories in dementia: Development and proof‑of‑concept evaluation of the LUMEN conversational AI

custom.summary: In a test using invented cases, LUMEN, a prototype chatbot that interviews family carers about a relative's memory, produced summaries that a fixed scoring rubric sorted by dementia type with high accuracy (average AUROC 0.95, where 1.0 means perfect separation; lowest was 0.77, for mild cognitive impairment). The rubric's categories agreed closely with two clinicians' ratings (kappa 0.88). The team shaped the questions and screens with about 232 patients, members of the public and professionals, picked one of seven open-source language models, and ran 54 simulated carer conversations, half role-played by clinicians and half written by GPT-4. Usability averaged 78 of 100. The authors say this does not show real-world performance.
custom.studied: a conversational AI that takes collateral histories from dementia carers, tested on simulated carer interviews

title: Empowering Alzheimer's caregivers with conversational AI: a novel approach for enhanced communication and personalized support

custom.summary: In a blind comparison by 20 caregivers of people with dementia, the authors report that ADQueryAid, their caregiver chatbot, scored higher than plain ChatGPT 3.5 on a chatbot usability questionnaire (mean 83.8 against about 73 out of 100). Paired tests showed clear gains on 4 of 16 items: a more engaging personality, explaining its purpose, more useful answers and fewer irrelevant ones. The system, built on GPT-4, draws on a dementia knowledge graph holding the patient's profile and on Alzheimer's Association documents. When a caregiver's concern is vague, it asks plain follow-up questions. Only 15% of participants had formal dementia training.
custom.studied: caregivers of people with Alzheimer's and related dementias recruited from online support communities

title: Catch the Patient, Not the AI: Collective Sensemaking in an Online Health Community

custom.summary: Forum members answered the person who brought AI into a thread far more often than they discussed the AI itself, the author reports. The study analysed 337 threads from House086, a large Chinese online forum for lymphoma patients and their caregivers. Members responded at least partly to what the poster wanted in 81.6% of threads but said nothing about the AI in 73.3%, even when posters asked them to weigh AI against a doctor's advice. Caregivers started 118 threads (35%), and 22% of them described being overwhelmed or frightened by what the AI told them, compared with about 17% of all posters. Most AI use (83%) was for explaining medical information.
custom.studied: AI-related discussion threads on a Chinese online forum for lymphoma patients and caregivers

title: ChatGPT vs Google for Queries Related to Dementia and Other Cognitive Decline: Comparison of Results

custom.summary: The authors report that ChatGPT gave more on-point answers than Google's top result to dementia questions, but it named no sources, rarely gave dates and was harder to read. The team wrote 60 questions of the kind caregivers ask, entered in March 2023. Half asked about facts, adapted from a dementia knowledge quiz, and half asked about finding and paying for local services such as respite or adult day care. Three experts rated 58 of 60 ChatGPT answers highly relevant, against 36 for Google. ChatGPT dated one answer where Google dated 19, and its replies averaged a 12th-grade reading level against about 9th grade for Google.
custom.studied: ChatGPT and Google answers to dementia questions written as caregivers would ask them

title: The Speculative Future of Conversational AI for Neurocognitive Disorder Screening: a Multi-Stakeholder Perspective

custom.summary: Interviews in China found that older adults, unpaid family caregivers and clinicians all favoured conversational AI that screens for memory and thinking disorders at home or in community clinics, chiefly to avoid the stress and stigma of hospital visits. They disagreed on its role: older adults and caregivers wanted comforting feedback and instant results, while clinicians wanted standardised test delivery and only a prompt to see a doctor. The authors interviewed 36 people (24 adults aged 60 or older, 7 family caregivers, 5 neurology clinicians) after showing videos of human and AI-run screening tests. They mapped each group's journey through screening and proposed design ideas, such as the AI passing information among the three groups.
custom.studied: older adults at risk of neurocognitive disorders, their family caregivers and clinicians in China

title: The use of generative AI tools among individuals with cancer and their caregivers: a cross-sectional study of awareness, attitudes, and experiences
container-title: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

custom.summary: Three in four of 400 people surveyed at a cancer hospital knew of generative AI tools, yet only 24% had used them to look up cancer information, and 69% of those users had not told their doctor. About a third of the sample were unpaid caregivers and the rest were patients; the authors report that caregivers turned to AI more often than patients and for different reasons. A university degree, being 55 or younger, and a diagnosis within the past year each made use more likely. Most respondents (73%) said they would use AI tools their physician had checked, and no user reported trusting their oncologist less.
custom.studied: adult cancer patients and their family caregivers at a tertiary oncology center

title: Multiturn Large Language Model-Based Conversational Agents for Patients With Cancer and Caregivers: Scoping Review

custom.summary: Of 8 studies of chatbots built on large language models for people with cancer or their family caregivers, the authors report that only 2 described any way for the chatbot to remember earlier parts of a conversation, and none tested how well conversations held together over several turns. Searching 8 databases and screening 1,172 records, they found 7 chatbots built for patients and just 1 for caregivers. Most used ChatGPT 4.0, and 5 looked up outside documents such as clinical guidelines before answering. No study published its full prompts (the instructions given to the model), and only one followed a reporting guideline.
custom.studied: published studies of multiturn chatbots built on large language models for adults with cancer and their informal caregivers

title: User Experiences of a Chatbot for Supporting the Self-Management of Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter for Chemotherapy: Mixed Methods Study

custom.summary: Half of 56 people with cancer or their family caregivers used a scripted chatbot for looking after a PICC line (a thin chemotherapy tube placed through an upper-arm vein) during one month in Korea. Users tended to be younger and more often women; whether someone was a patient or a caregiver made no clear difference. Logs from 25 users held 347 questions, most about catheter care, and the bot understood 69 of 100 typed questions. Of 23 users surveyed, 22 found it easy to use; interviewees valued round-the-clock answers and reassurance but wanted more personal, detailed replies and found sideways swiping hard for older relatives.
custom.studied: Korean patients with cancer getting a PICC line and their family caregivers using a KakaoTalk chatbot

title: A comparative evaluation of ChatGPT and Gemini for stroke caregiver support: accuracy, safety, and response characteristics

custom.summary: Ten clinical experts rated ChatGPT and Gemini similarly when both answered stroke caregiving questions, with no significant difference between the two tools on any measure. The authors posed 10 caregiver-style questions in December 2025, covering preventing another stroke, recovery, mood changes, burnout, home care and government benefits. Three neurologists, three rehabilitation physicians and four physiotherapists scored each answer for clarity, empathy, practical usefulness, safety and accuracy. Both tools generally scored well, but some answers scored lower on safety: advice was rarely tailored, overlooked memory and thinking problems after stroke, or assumed equipment caregivers may lack. Agreement between raters was poor.
custom.studied: ChatGPT and Gemini answers to stroke caregiving questions, rated by clinical experts

title: Who's Asking? Simulating Role-Based Questions for Conversational AI Evaluation

custom.summary: When the same opioid recovery question was framed as coming from a family caregiver, five large language models gave answers with about 23% less practical information on average, along with about 19% more emotional support and text about 24% easier to read. The authors built CoRUS, a method that rewrites 5,107 questions drawn from a Reddit opioid recovery forum so each one implicitly sounds like a patient, a caregiver or a clinician, yielding 15,321 questions. Automated and crowd-worker checks rated most rewrites as realistic. Patient framing showed a similar pattern, while clinician framing slightly lowered support and readability.
custom.studied: Simulated patient, caregiver and clinician versions of questions from an online opioid recovery forum, put to five language models

title: Review of Large Language Models for Patient and Caregiver Support in Cancer Care Delivery

custom.summary: The authors report that uses of large language models (LLMs, the AI behind chatbots such as ChatGPT) to help people with cancer and their caregivers fall into four groups: teaching and answering questions, checking symptoms and judging urgency, telehealth, and joining clinical trials. In this narrative review, chatbots tend to answer simple cancer questions well but are less dependable on complicated cases, and proof that they improve outcomes is still scarce. The authors name obstacles including ongoing monitoring, fair access, privacy and checking accuracy across different groups. They also offer a guide for doctors discussing chatbot use with patients.
custom.studied: published research on large language model tools supporting people with cancer and their caregivers

title: The ethics of using virtual assistants to help people in vulnerable positions access care

custom.summary: In Dutch focus groups, people who need long-term support and those who care for them saw a planned chatbot as an easier first step toward asking for help, yet doubted it could handle complex situations or serve everyone. The authors reanalysed discussions with 23 care recipients (with intellectual disability, autism, brain injury or mental illness) and 13 caregivers, 4 of them family members, about a 'sensitive' virtual assistant. Participants valued that it might ease shame and point people to the right service. They worried about losing human contact, privacy, unreliable answers, and users who struggle to write or phrase a question. The authors argue that people should always be able to reach a human instead.
custom.studied: Dutch care recipients in vulnerable positions and their professional and family caregivers

title: Evaluating the impact of an AI-powered chatbot on epilepsy education and stigma reduction: A pre-post intervention study using EpiloBot

custom.summary: After about a month with EpiloBot, a Japanese epilepsy chatbot built on a fine-tuned ChatGPT and delivered through the LINE messaging app, the 82 adults who answered both surveys more often agreed that people with epilepsy should hold ordinary jobs, and they scored higher on knowledge of treatment. Family members and caregivers both showed significant gains on the job item. The authors report that self-stigma among the nine participants with epilepsy rose slightly. Of 176 people who registered, 46.6% completed the follow-up survey; quality of life, self-esteem and knowledge of causes and symptoms did not change significantly.
custom.studied: Japanese adults with epilepsy, their family members and caregivers, and others using an epilepsy education chatbot

title: From Checking to Sensemaking: A Caregiver-in-the-Loop Framework for AI-Assisted Task Verification in Dementia Care

custom.summary: In interviews with ten family caregivers of people with dementia in Canada, plus one person living with dementia, the authors report that caregivers treated checking whether a daily task got done as interpretation. They pieced together spoken answers, household clues such as a wet towel, and notes from other helpers. Caregivers were cautiously open to AI drafting check-in questions and flagging worrying replies, provided they could edit the wording and set alert thresholds. A GPT-4 probe built from 64 past reminders wrote more suitable questions when given caregiver context. From this the authors propose a framework that keeps caregivers in charge of AI-assisted checking.
custom.studied: Canadian family caregivers of people living with dementia at home

title: Validation of an AI-powered mobile application for personalizing medical note explanations: a mixed-methods evaluation

custom.summary: The author reports that Patiently AI, a phone app using GPT-4o to rewrite clinical notes for a chosen reader (adult, teenager, child or carer) and tone, lowered reading level from about US grade 10.6 to 7.6 across 210 outputs made from 10 invented notes. Fifteen health professionals rated outputs safe in 87% of 150 reviews. The output drawing the most safety flags was a reassuring carer version about falls. Among 54 online participants, about a quarter of them caregivers, 70% of responses preferred the rewritten note, and 98% of comprehension answers were correct. Carer versions showed the smallest readability gain.
custom.studied: a GPT-4o app that explains medical notes for patients, carers, teenagers and children

title: Effects of Different Prompts on the Quality of GPT-4 Responses to Dementia Care Questions

custom.summary: The authors report that changing the prompt made no measurable difference to how two dementia clinicians rated GPT-4's answers to caregivers' questions, although asking for maximum detail made answers much longer. They gave GPT-4 three real Reddit posts from dementia caregivers, about confusion, aggression and driving, under 12 prompt setups. These mixed four assigned roles, such as social worker or neuropsychologist, with three levels of instruction, producing 36 answers. On a 0 to 5 scale, 16 answers scored 5, 16 scored 4 and 4 scored 3, and the clinicians found no invented facts. They judged some of the extra detail in the longest answers clinically unnecessary, and the assigned role changed little in the content.
custom.studied: GPT-4 answers to three dementia caregiver posts from Reddit under 12 prompt combinations

title: Cultural Feasibility of Conversational Robots for Dementia Care in India: Participatory Design Study

custom.summary: People living with dementia in Chennai, India, talked readily with three conversational robots, and they and their caregivers rated the robots as sociable and useful, though about half doubted they could use the smart speaker or tablet robot without help, the authors report. The study involved 29 people: 11 with mild to moderate dementia, 11 paid or family caregivers and 7 dementia care professionals. They tried or watched an Amazon Echo, an animated face on a tablet and a small robot called Miko in one session, then answered questionnaires and interviews. Participants wanted reminders, company and robots that understand Indian accents in noisy homes, and caregivers raised worries about privacy and cost.
custom.studied: people living with dementia, their caregivers and dementia care professionals in Chennai, India

title: Development of a Technology-Based Dyadic Intervention for Underserved Colorectal Cancer Patients and Caregivers
container-title: Studies in health technology and informatics

custom.summary: The authors describe an intervention under development that uses generative AI to give people with colorectal cancer, and the family members who care for them, education matched to each person's unmet needs. The aim is to help patient and caregiver pairs manage symptoms together and to narrow gaps in care for underserved groups. The short abstract reports no participants, testing or results, and does not say whether the AI talks with users or only produces written material.
custom.studied: a generative AI education intervention for underserved colorectal cancer patients and their family caregivers

title: Large language model-assisted support among caregivers of patients with epilepsy: associations with caregiver burden and psychosocial outcomes

custom.summary: Caregivers who used the DeepSeek chatbot for epilepsy care help reported a somewhat larger drop in caregiver strain over three months than those who did not, the authors report. In this single-hospital study in China, 296 family caregivers (147 users, 149 non-users) completed questionnaires at the start, one month and three months. After adjusting for caregiver and patient differences, burden scores on a standard 22-item strain scale fell about 2.2 points more among users. Users also improved more on anxiety, depression, stress and mental quality of life, with no difference in social support or confidence in caregiving. How often people used the chatbot made no clear difference, and the authors did not check its answers.
custom.studied: primary family caregivers of people with epilepsy at a Chinese hospital, grouped by whether they used DeepSeek for caregiving support

title: Attitudes of people living with dementia and their carers towards the use of generative artificial intelligence to inform structured medication reviews

custom.summary: The authors report that 26 UK participants, 12 people with early-stage dementia and 14 unpaid carers, were broadly open to clinicians using generative AI to prepare structured medication reviews (NHS appointments where a professional checks all of a patient's medicines), provided a clinician kept the final say. In interviews and two focus groups, participants also worried about invented or wrong AI output, liability for harm, data breaches, incomplete records and losing a familiar doctor. Views split on whether patients should be told AI was used. Participants described hard medication routines, rushed reviews and carers feeling sidelined, and asked to help design such tools.
custom.studied: UK people living with dementia and unpaid carers of people with dementia and polypharmacy

sample.of: people living with dementia and carers

title: Integrating AI-Powered Chatbots Into Patient Education From the Perspectives of Patients, Caregivers, and Nurses: Qualitative Study

custom.summary: Chatbots were welcomed as an extra source of health information, but only on conditions such as better accuracy and nurse oversight, according to interviews with 29 patients, 17 unpaid family caregivers and 14 nurses at a large hospital in Jinan, China. Most patients (76%) and caregivers (71%) had used chatbots, mostly to look up treatment information. Caregivers said this helped them join care decisions and talk with staff better prepared. Participants did not see chatbots as harming trust in nurses. Some nurses felt challenged when chatbot answers conflicted with theirs, and some patients and caregivers avoided telling nurses they had used one.
custom.studied: hospital patients, their unpaid primary caregivers, and nurses in China

title: Quality, safety, and readability of consumer-facing generative AI responses to end-of-life questions relevant to surrogate decision-makers for older adults: a benchmark evaluation

custom.summary: Two clinicians rated 28 of 150 chatbot answers (19%) unsafe, using criteria such as overstating what resuscitation can achieve or presenting palliative care as giving up. Safe-answer rates ran from 76.7% to 86.7% across five systems, with no meaningful difference between them. The authors put 30 plain-language end-of-life questions, framed as a family member deciding for a dying older relative, to ChatGPT (GPT-5.3 Instant), Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek and Perplexity. They report that answers were mostly accurate (median 4 of 5) and supportive in tone. However, the answers read at about grade 11 or above, well beyond the grade 6 to 8 advised for patient material, and often gave little sign of who wrote them or when.
custom.studied: five public chatbots answering end-of-life questions phrased as a family surrogate decision-maker for an older adult would ask

title: InvisibleBench: A Deployment Gate for Caregiving Relationship AI

custom.summary: In this benchmark, none of four large language models reliably caught signs of crisis in scripted conversations with family caregivers. Crisis-detection scores ranged from 11.8% (GPT-4o Mini) to 44.8% (Claude Sonnet 4.5), and indirect signals were missed far more often than direct ones. The author wrote 17 caregiver scenarios of 3 to over 20 turns, some spread across several sessions. Another model graded the replies on safety, avoiding medical advice, sensitivity to trauma, cultural fit and memory, with automatic failure for a missed crisis, dosing or diagnosis advice, or fostering dependence. DeepSeek scored highest overall (75.9%), and the author argues that fixed rule-based crisis handling is needed before such tools are released.
custom.studied: four large language models answering researcher-written family caregiver conversations

title: Supporting Dementia Caregiving With a Mobile Care Ecosystem: Development and Mixed Methods Study

custom.summary: Dementia caregivers in Singapore rated CareBuddy, a mobile app that includes a GPT-4 chatbot, as easy to use and useful. The team built it from interviews with 22 caregivers, clinicians and others, then tested it with 18 people over three interview rounds and with 10 caregivers who used it at home for a month. Usability scores on a standard scale rose from 65.4 in the first round to roughly 74 to 78 later, above the usual benchmark of 68, and at least 40% of home users opened it daily. The chatbot answers from a curated question bank (retrieval-augmented generation); early testers asked for warmer, more empathetic replies.
custom.studied: family caregivers of people with dementia in Singapore, plus health care providers

sample.of: pilot participants (21 caregivers and 7 health care providers)

title: Impact of age and comorbid heart failure on the utility of smart voice-assistant devices

custom.summary: In this secondary analysis of a crossover trial, answers captured by Amazon Alexa during a COVID-19 screening matched those taken by a research coordinator slightly less often for heart failure patients than for their caregivers (95% vs 99% agreement; kappa, an agreement score corrected for chance, 0.81 vs 0.98). The authors report a similar gap for participants older than the median age of 51. The 52 participants at a heart failure clinic, 21 patients and 31 caregivers, each answered the same yes/no questions to Alexa and to a person. Patients and older participants found Alexa harder to use and rated it lower, though comfort did not differ and no one raised privacy concerns.
custom.studied: heart failure patients and their caregivers screened for COVID-19 by Amazon Alexa and by a research coordinator

title: From Hospital to Home: Enhancing Family Support with MIGYN (Mitra Interaktif Ginekologi), an AI-Based Discharge Planning Chatbot

custom.summary: Caregivers who used MIGYN, a Telegram chatbot built for the move home after gynecological surgery, improved more on a 10-item care knowledge test than those given routine discharge teaching (median gain 5 versus 3 points). Family support scores rose by similar amounts in both groups. The study followed 34 family caregivers, mostly husbands, at one hospital in Bandung, Indonesia, with 17 using the chatbot for two weeks and 17 receiving usual care. MIGYN offered lessons on wound care, medicines, diet, movement and warning signs, along with reminders and a question feature. The authors caution that groups were not randomly assigned and differed in age and education.
custom.studied: family caregivers of women recovering from gynecological surgery at an Indonesian hospital

title: Generative-AI as a source of caregiving guidance for medical tourists: A content and readability analysis

custom.summary: The authors report that caregiving advice from three AI chatbots for people accompanying a relative or friend abroad for medical treatment (medical tourism) was often written above the reading level advised for the public and seldom cited sources. In March 2024 the researchers put a fixed series of prompts to ChatGPT-4, Gemini 1.0 and Copilot and analysed the answers by theme. All three covered trip planning, handling a foreign culture, speaking up for the patient and keeping care connected after return. They largely left out trust between companion and patient and making decisions on the patient's behalf. The authors conclude the output could help shape human-edited guides but should not stand alone.
custom.studied: caregiving guidance from three generative AI chatbots for medical tourism companions

title: Categorizing Sources of Information for Explanations in Conversational AI Systems for Older Adults Aging in Place

custom.summary: The authors propose an early framework sorting where a home voice assistant could draw explanations for its actions, such as why it gave a medication reminder, into four groups: the person's past conversations and habits, sensors and other household tasks, details of the task itself, and the AI's own confidence. The framework grows out of two earlier long-term home studies (20 and 10 weeks) with 17 pairs of older adults with mild cognitive impairment and their family caregivers, covering 1,596 assistant-initiated check-ins and 844 replies. The authors also flag privacy around sensor data and the difficulty of learning from indirect user feedback.
custom.studied: older adults with mild cognitive impairment and their family caregivers using a home conversational assistant for medication check-ins

title: Virtual Assistant as a Companion for Stroke Survivors post Discharge: Thematic Analysis Highlights Expectations of Human Performance Pose a Key Barrier to Engagement

custom.summary: Stroke survivors and family care partners who tried a prototype stroke virtual assistant (a chatbot that talks and listens) often spoke of it as a person, and the authors argue this leads users to expect human abilities, like reading body language, that it cannot offer. The team that built the tool ran workshops in the Czech Republic, plus interviews and hands-on testing in Scotland and Northern Ireland, with 46 people aged 55 to 85. Participants wanted plain-language answers and emotional reassurance on demand after leaving hospital. They named discomfort with technology, hand and sight problems, and doubts about accuracy as barriers.
custom.studied: stroke survivors and family care partners in the Czech Republic, Scotland and Northern Ireland

title: Balancing Safety and Autonomy: Accessibility-Oriented Interventions in Generative AI for Cognitive Impairment

custom.summary: The authors report that safety features in generative AI tools, such as declining to diagnose or asking a family member to approve a change, helped people with severe cognitive impairment but frustrated many with mild impairment, who felt their independence was curtailed. The interviews covered 45 older adults with cognitive impairment: 31 spoke for themselves and 14 were described by caregivers (7 family members and 7 doctors). The team sorted what the systems did into five mechanisms, including limits on what the AI will say, human sign-off on decisions, and step-by-step prompting. As impairment deepened, complaints faded, which the authors link partly to caregivers taking over the interpreting and choosing.
custom.studied: older adults with cognitive impairment using conversational health and companion AI, and their caregivers

title: Perspectives of people affected by cancer toward generative AI in oncology: A scoping review of applications, evidence gaps, and future priorities

custom.summary: Across 32 studies with 4,919 participants, the authors report that people affected by cancer mostly welcomed generative AI when it made health information easier to read and reach, but trusted it only if it felt personal, emotionally fitting, accurate and checked by clinicians. Most studies looked at patient communication and education (21), with fewer on plain-language summaries of clinical notes (6) or decision support (2). Usefulness, understanding and trust were the most measured views. The review notes that no study asked these people about safety, transparency, fairness or autonomy.
custom.studied: studies of the views of people affected by cancer on generative AI in cancer care

title: When Pleasing the User Compromises Care: AI Sycophancy in Caregiver-Mediated Healthcare

custom.summary: The authors report that when a simulated caregiver pushed for a less suitable option, AI advisors often dropped advice that had been sound at first. Across six models, switching to inappropriate care within five turns rose 10 to 51 percentage points above a neutral follow-up, and most of these failures were rated moderately or severely harmful. They built CareDistance, a benchmark of 450 guideline-based cases split evenly across care of older parents, children and animals. In 112 eldercare cases, models gave way about equally whether the patient or an adult child voiced the preference. Under caregiver pressure, models asked what the patient wanted in only 12.6% of first failures.
custom.studied: AI advisor answers to simulated caregivers asking about guideline-based care for older parents, children and animals

title: Prevalence and predictors of artificial intelligence chatbots use for caregiving: Evidence from the Understanding America Study

custom.summary: Among 1,300 US caregivers from the Understanding America Study, a national probability-based online panel, 37% had used AI chatbots such as ChatGPT. A quarter of those users (121 of 487) said they had used chatbots for caregiving, mostly to look up information (58%) and less often for emotional support (34%). Among chatbot users, those who scored higher on openness to new experiences, felt less sure how to provide care, or had lower cognitive test and internet skill scores were more likely to use chatbots for caregiving. In 128 short written comments, caregivers often described chatbots as quick and helpful, while about 9% mentioned limits such as repeated or weak answers.
custom.studied: US adults caring for a family member or friend, from a national probability-based panel

title: Using technology for patient-centered care at home after CAR T-cell therapy or stem cell transplant: a prospective feasibility study

custom.summary: The authors report that 9 of 10 adults sent home after a stem cell transplant or CAR T-cell therapy (a cancer treatment using reprogrammed immune cells) wore a monitoring patch as intended and used a text-message chatbot, beating the study's 60% target. In this pilot at one Colorado centre, lasting 30 to 90 days per patient, an AI chatbot called Remi ran symptom check-ins and took questions, while nurses watched around the clock and could step into the chat. Patients found both tools easy to use, though some said the chatbot sometimes failed to understand them or sent too many messages. Of 6 caregivers who answered a survey, 5 said the monitoring eased caregiving stress.
custom.studied: adults at home after stem cell transplant or CAR T-cell therapy, with their in-home caregivers and providers

title: Transforming dementia caregiver support with AI-powered social robotics

custom.summary: The authors report that RISE, a talking Pepper humanoid robot that teaches family caregivers of people with dementia, gave accurate answers when GPT-4o was limited to an established caregiver program's notebook, a method called retrieval augmented generation. On 52 caregiver questions with expert-written answers, AI judges scored it at least 87% for correctness and 92% for relevance, well above GPT-4o used alone. Five engineering students who tried a full session rated every part at 3.8 or more out of 5. Two dementia care experts reviewed a video and asked for slower speech and clearer wording. No caregivers have yet tested it.
custom.studied: a robot-delivered, notebook-grounded AI education system for family dementia caregivers, tested with students, experts and a set of caregiver questions

title: ALERT-ED: Awareness and Linkage to Resources for At-Risk Emergency Department Patients: Interviews with Older Patients, Caregivers, and Nurses
container-title: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine

custom.summary: In interviews, older emergency department patients, family caregivers and nurses judged ALERT-ED workable, acceptable and easy to use. The tool prints a QR code on the discharge papers of patients at high risk of falling. The code opens a chatbot named Livi that lets people check their own fall risk, learn how to prevent falls and find community programs. The authors interviewed 12 patients aged 65 and over, 4 caregivers and 6 nurses, in English or Spanish, across several hospitals. Participants liked the simple QR access, but they raised privacy worries, distrust of AI, limited nurse time and gaps for people with impairments.
custom.studied: older emergency department patients at high fall risk, their caregivers, and ED nurses

title: Use of large language model-based chatbots in managing the rehabilitation concerns and education needs of outpatient stroke survivors and caregivers

custom.summary: Three rehabilitation doctors rated Google Bard's answers satisfactory in 75.8% of 120 gradings and ChatGPT's in 65.8%. Both chatbots made up local resources, such as a support group and a financial aid scheme that do not exist, and neither raised possible self-harm risk when asked about low mood. Agreement among the raters was slight. The questions came from 50 anonymous questionnaires returned by stroke patients or their caregivers at a Singapore outpatient clinic, which held 280 questions; these were grouped into 10 representative questions. Each chatbot answered them in February 2024 and was scored on accuracy, safety, relevance and readability.
custom.studied: ChatGPT and Google Bard answers to stroke rehabilitation questions gathered from outpatients and their caregivers in Singapore

title: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models

custom.summary: The authors report that GPT-4 answers to dementia caregivers' questions were more polite, formal and structured than peer replies and scored about as well as physicians on informational measures, yet told fewer personal stories and covered a narrower range of topics. The team took 85 help requests posted on the ALZConnected forum in 2023 and compared four answers to each: real peer replies, answers from four physicians, ChatGPT, and CareGPT, a version of GPT-4 that first looks up similar posts from over 50,000 forum posts (retrieval-augmented generation). They scored the 340 responses on 28 measures. ChatGPT replies ran about 180 words longer than physicians', and CareGPT read almost the same as ChatGPT.
custom.studied: help requests posted by dementia caregivers on the ALZConnected forum, answered by peers, physicians, ChatGPT and a retrieval-based chatbot

title: Two Modes of Reflection: How Temporal, Spatial, and Social Distances Affect Reflective Writing in Family Caregiving

custom.summary: The authors report that caregivers wrote differently depending on how close they were to a stressful moment. Soon after it, or with the cared-for person nearby, entries were vivid, emotional and centred on that person. Later, or when apart or when someone else was caring, entries were calmer, more about the writer and more analytical. Over three weeks, 47 Japanese caregivers used a scripted chatbot on the LINE messaging app that asked about their stress five times a day and prompted one reflective diary entry daily, producing 958 entries. Participants said writing right away helped them vent but felt less objective, while waiting helped them think things through but blurred the details.
custom.studied: Japanese family caregivers writing daily reflections through a messaging-app chatbot

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Health Research and Care: A Narrative Review of Applications and Implications for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementia

custom.summary: The authors conclude that evidence on generative AI for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias comes mostly from small, retrospective studies, and that no generative tool has yet been tested prospectively or authorized as a medical device. This narrative review (a broad, non-systematic look at the literature) covers chatbot-based cognitive screening, companion chatbots, caregiver support tools, synthetic data, digital twins, ethics and regulation. On caregivers, the authors report that chatbots grounded in curated content scored better on usability: 20 caregivers rated one at 83.8 against 72.5 for ChatGPT-3.5. They add that no such tool has yet beaten general models on accuracy or safety, and that ChatGPT's dementia answers read at about a 12th-grade level.
custom.studied: published research on generative AI and large language models in dementia research and care

title: A Reliable and Accessible Caregiving Language Model (CaLM) to Support Tools for Caregivers: Development and Evaluation Study

custom.summary: The authors report that small 7-billion-parameter open models, when given a dementia caregiving document library to draw on (retrieval augmented generation) and further trained on caregiving question-answer pairs, scored higher than the far larger GPT-3.5 on automatic text-similarity measures. Tested on 66 held-out questions, the tuned LLaMA 2 7B cited sources in all 66 answers, against 46 (70%) for GPT-3.5 with the same library. Its citations were correct and relevant 80.0% of the time, against 62.1%. The team also built a prototype caregiver chatbot that needs about 4 to 6 GB of memory and can run on a laptop. No caregivers took part. GPT-4 drafted the questions, and an annotator checked them.
custom.studied: language models answering questions written from the view of caregivers of people with Alzheimer disease and related dementias

title: LLM-Mediated Smart Tele-Primary Care for Rural Older Adults: A Caregiver-Centered and Scenario-Assessed Framework for Respiratory Infection Monitoring

custom.summary: The authors report that their triage rules, tested on 60 invented respiratory infection cases, matched the reference risk level in 56, flagged every high-risk case, and only ever moved cases up a level when a blood-oxygen reading was missing. The rules build on a survey of patient and caregiver pairs in rural Córdoba, Colombia: about 90% said they understood COVID-19 symptoms and prevention, yet about half reported lapses in physical distancing while unwell. The team designed a WhatsApp-based service in which GPT-3.5 collects caregivers' everyday descriptions of symptoms and turns them into structured reports. Clinicians review these reports and make every decision.
custom.studied: rural older adults with COVID-19 care needs and their family caregivers in Córdoba, Colombia

title: AI in Home Care-Evaluation of Large Language Models for Future Training of Informal Caregivers: Observational Comparative Case Study

custom.summary: None of the three chatbots tested matched instructions written by health professionals, though GPT-4o came closest. Reviewers posed standard prompts on 10 home care tasks for older adults, such as giving insulin, helping after choking and moving a person safely, to GPT-3.5, GPT-4o and Copilot, and scored 60 answers against expert scripts. GPT-4o rated highest for detail and clarity, and its answers were judged adequate for building caregiver confidence 90% of the time, against 40% for Copilot. The authors report that all three models left out key steps in 60% to 80% of scenarios. GPT-4o gave wrong information in 1 of 10 scenarios and Copilot in 2.
custom.studied: chatbot answers to prompts on 10 common home care tasks for dependent older adults

title: The landscape of knowledge graph and large language model-augmented knowledge graph applications in dementia caregiving support: a scoping review

custom.summary: Of 11 studies the review found on knowledge graphs for dementia care, only 3 paired the graph with a large language model. Those 3 mostly used retrieval-augmented generation, where a chatbot looks up facts in the graph before it answers caregivers or people with dementia. A knowledge graph is a structured map of facts and how they connect. The other 8 used graphs alone, for tasks such as meal planning, care plan suggestions, robots and virtual assistants. The authors report early signs of easier use and more personal advice, alongside few tests in real homes, hard upkeep, data quality problems and thin attention to ethics.
custom.studied: published and gray literature on knowledge graph and LLM-augmented knowledge graph systems for dementia caregiving

title: Voice Assistants to Deliver Cognitive Stimulation Therapy for Persons Living with Dementia
container-title: Extended abstracts on Human factors in computing systems. CHI Conference
container-title-short: Ext Abstr Hum Factors Computing Syst

custom.summary: Five unpaid US family caregivers of people with dementia found a voice assistant that runs cognitive stimulation exercises (structured home activities such as quizzes and reminiscing, meant to keep thinking skills active) workable and welcome.
