All five doubted the person they cared for could use it alone. The authors built CSTalk, an Amazon Alexa skill on a screen device that uses GPT-4o for open conversation, including a quiz on whether common sayings are true. Caregivers tried two sessions over Zoom, then were interviewed. They asked for content suited to dementia stage and personal interests, sessions shared with the caregiver, training, avoidance of upsetting topics, pictures, and protection against privacy risks and scams.
custom.studied: US unpaid family caregivers of people living with dementia trying an LLM-powered Alexa prototype

title: Evolution of Chatbots as an Educational and Supportive Digital Intervention for Family Caregivers of People With Dementia: Protocol for a Systematic Integrative Review

custom.summary: This protocol describes a planned review of studies on chatbots built to teach and support family members caring for someone with dementia; it reports no results yet. The authors plan to search seven databases plus grey literature, include primary studies of any design, and pool trials in a meta-analysis only if enough comparable ones turn up. The review will ask which caregiver needs these chatbots address, how they were built, how well they work, what got in the way, and what ethical and safety concerns came up, judged against World Health Organization guidance. An integrative review combines qualitative and quantitative evidence in a single synthesis.
custom.studied: planned review of studies on chatbots for family caregivers of people with dementia

title: Improving Patient-Reported End-of-Life Data Capture: A Pilot Mixed-Methods Evaluation of an Electronic Patient Reported Outcomes Chatbot Platform Using Messaging Applications From Bereaved Caregivers in Chile

custom.summary: The authors report that all 21 bereaved caregivers who registered finished a Spanish questionnaire on the quality of a relative's death through a chatbot on everyday messaging apps, and 20 of 21 also completed a follow-up interview. The single-group pilot in Chile invited 36 caregivers. Of the 15 lost before registering, 11 were lost to consent arrangements at the hospital. Half finished the questionnaire in 15 minutes or less and all within a day, and 13 of 20 (65%) replied within the planned window of 14 to 84 days after the death. Most respondents were the patient's adult children (70%) or spouses (15%).
custom.studied: bereaved family caregivers in Chile reporting on a relative's death via a messaging chatbot

title: Development of a Rule-Based Chatbot for Supporting Family Caregivers After Psychiatric Hospital Discharge: An Exploratory Qualitative Study in Indonesia

custom.summary: Interviews with three family caregivers and five mental health professionals at a psychiatric hospital in West Java, plus WhatsApp consultation records from 67 families and five discharge sheets, found that caregivers lacked knowledge about medicines, relapse warning signs and home care. They also carried heavy emotional and money strain, and the hospital's online consultation line was slow to reply. The authors turned these nine themes into KJOL-ITEUNGBOT, a scripted chatbot that guides users through menus of set questions (a decision tree) and refers complex cases to staff. Six experts reviewed the design, and the authors report it has not yet been tested for usability or effect.
custom.studied: family caregivers of people with severe mental illness after psychiatric discharge, and hospital mental health staff, in Indonesia

title: Performance and usability of retrieval-augmented large language models for stroke patient and caregiver support

custom.summary: Grounding three large language models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7, Qwen3) in a curated stroke knowledge base raised expert ratings for accuracy and completeness, but two of the three gave answers rated harder for lay readers to follow. The authors built a retrieval system that looks up guideline passages before answering in Chinese. They tested it on 184 exam questions and on 30 everyday patient and caregiver questions scored by three clinicians. In a usability test of the GPT-4o version, 20 people (12 stroke survivors, 8 family caregivers) each asked 5 to 10 questions and gave a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.75 out of 100, which the authors class as good.
custom.studied: a retrieval-based stroke question-answering assistant for patients and family caregivers in China

sample.of: stroke survivors and family caregivers in usability testing

title: An Evidence-Based IT Program With Chatbot to Support Caregiving and Clinical Care for People With Dementia: The CareHeroes Development and Usability Pilot

custom.summary: Among the features of CareHeroes, a web app for family caregivers of people with dementia, the educational chatbot was used most: 44 of 169 recorded caregiver actions. The chatbot matches a typed question to stored answers taken from a dementia caregiving guidebook. In a pilot at two US memory clinics, 21 caregivers enrolled and 13 completed both the starting and 3-month interviews. The authors report that depression scores fell significantly by 3 months (from an average of 1.67 to 1.08 on a two-question screen), while anxiety and overall distress did not change significantly. Recruitment and retention suffered during COVID-19.
custom.studied: family caregivers of people with dementia at two US memory clinics using a web app with an educational chatbot

title: Evaluation of ChatGPT's responses to information needs and information seeking of dementia patients

custom.summary: Family caregivers of people with advanced dementia rated ChatGPT's answers more favourably than clinicians did: an average of 3.77 out of 5 against 3.13. The authors built 118 questions from caregiver information needs found in 22 earlier studies and put them to ChatGPT in April 2023. Fifteen family caregivers and 15 neurologists or specialist nurses in Tehran, Iran, rated the answers and were interviewed. The gap between the groups was widest on clinical topics such as treatment, prognosis and medicines. Both groups liked the speed and ease of use, and clinicians wanted an expert to check answers before anyone relied on them.
custom.studied: family caregivers and clinicians in Tehran rating ChatGPT answers to dementia care questions

title: Chatbot-Mediated Learning For Caregiving Relatives of People With Dementia: Empirical Findings and Didactical Implications For Mulitprofessional Health Care

custom.summary: Family caregivers of people with dementia told the researchers they would learn best from a chatbot giving short, clear answers fitted to their own situation, in text, pictures or video, that they could save or print and talk over with others. Answers lacking context, overly long or off the question were named as barriers. The German team interviewed 6 caregivers by video and reviewed 6 earlier studies, then used the findings to shape a scripted, keyword-driven chatbot on agitation in dementia. Each topic comes in a short and a long version, the bot suggests deeper reading, and it ends by prompting the caregiver to reflect.
custom.studied: German family caregivers of people with dementia, interviewed about learning with a chatbot

title: Patients and Caregivers Leveraging AI to Improve Their Health Care Journey: Case Study and Lessons Learned

custom.summary: A wife caring for her husband through a sudden loss of mobility from lower back pain reports that ChatGPT cut the time between getting his MRI report and acting on it from weeks to days. With a colleague, she describes four steps: pasting the de-identified report in for a plain-language reading and likely diagnoses, asking follow-up questions about two possible spine operations, having it condense portal records and her own notes into a one-page summary shared with doctors, therapists and the insurer, and drafting questions for the neurosurgeon. The authors add advice on checking answers against trusted health websites and a second chatbot, removing identifying details, and future portal features.
custom.studied: one spouse caregiver's use of ChatGPT during her husband's spinal care

title: Telemedicine and AI-Powered Chatbots: Potential and Challenges for Home Care Provided by Family Caregivers

custom.summary: In two small online surveys of family caregivers on a caregiving course in Germany, 97% said they would want a chatbot to give clear step-by-step setup help, all said ease of use mattered, and 77% rated emotional support from a chatbot as important. Only 41% said they would actually ask one for help with telemedicine. The first survey (23 caregivers, January 2025) covered telemedicine barriers such as connection faults and privacy worries. The second (39 caregivers, September 2025) covered AI chatbots. The authors stress that the chatbot answers reflect expectations, since many respondents had never used such systems, and that caregivers wanted chatbots to sit alongside human contact.
custom.studied: family caregivers attending a caregiving course in Germany

title: Development and feasibility testing of an AI-powered chatbot for early detection of caregiver burden: protocol for a mixed methods feasibility study

custom.summary: This protocol describes plans for BOTANIC, a chatbot on the Telegram messaging app that uses GPT-4 to chat with family caregivers and estimate how strained they are. No results are reported yet. The chatbot's questions draw on the Zarit Burden Interview, a standard caregiver strain questionnaire, and a separate text-analysis pipeline turns caregivers' free-text replies into a running burden score. The authors plan to enrol 20 caregivers of people with chronic illnesses at one Singapore hospital for 12 weeks. They will compare the chatbot's scores with standard questionnaires on burden, depression and anxiety, track usability and engagement, and interview participants about their experience.
custom.studied: Planned: informal caregivers of patients with chronic conditions at a Singapore public hospital

title: Effectiveness of Chatbot interventions for reducing caregiver burden: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis

custom.summary: This protocol lays out how the authors plan to pool randomized trials of fully automated chatbots meant to ease the strain on unpaid caregivers. It reports no results yet. The team will search eight databases and grey literature for trials up to December 2024. The main outcome is caregiver burden, measured mainly with the Zarit Burden Interview, a standard strain questionnaire. Mood, quality of life, confidence and the cared-for person's health are secondary outcomes. Two reviewers will each screen studies and rate bias, and the authors will test whether effects differ by caregiver, health condition and chatbot design. The review is registered with PROSPERO as CRD42024628606.
custom.studied: randomized trials of automated chatbots for informal caregivers (planned)

title: DementiaCare-Bench: A Modality-Validated Video Benchmark

custom.summary: The authors report that 12 current video-language models (AI that answers questions about video) scored up to 85% on a new dementia-care test, but mostly from clinical knowledge: six did best when shown no video at all, and accuracy dropped about 17 points on questions needing the clip's order of events. The benchmark holds 2,023 multiple-choice questions on 94 clips from 56 caregiver-training videos acted out by actors, covering nine kinds of behavioural symptoms of dementia such as agitation and wandering. Only 34.8% of questions turned out to need ordered frames, against 77.7% intended. A small fine-tuned model raised held-out accuracy from 83.6% to 93.1%.
custom.studied: video-language models answering questions about dementia caregiver-training videos

title: Mapping Caregiver Needs to AI Chatbot Design: Strengths and Gaps in Mental Health Support for Alzheimer's and Dementia Caregivers

custom.summary: Fifteen of 16 US family caregivers of people with dementia called a GPT-4o chatbot helpful or very helpful after trying it on common stressors such as emotional distress, burnout and difficult behaviour. The researchers built the chatbot, named Carey, to prompt reactions and interviewed each caregiver for an hour while they chatted with it. Caregivers valued its round-the-clock availability and calm, non-judging tone. They doubted whether its information could be trusted, found its tailoring shallow and some replies repetitive, wanted it to ask questions back, and noted it had no way to hand off a crisis. The authors turn these findings into design suggestions such as citing sources and giving users privacy controls.
custom.studied: US family caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, recruited from online communities

title: Comparative Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots in Delivering Palliative Care Education to Intensive Care Unit Caregivers- A Cross-platform Analysis: A Brief Communication
container-title: Indian journal of critical care medicine : peer-reviewed, official publication of Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine

custom.summary: Free versions of ChatGPT and Google Gemini each wrote a palliative care leaflet for families of a seriously ill patient in intensive care, and both texts needed about a 13th-grade reading level, which the authors describe as college level. On PEMAT-P, a standard checklist for patient handouts, both scored 91.7% for ease of understanding and 80% for giving clear steps to act on. Seven physician reviewers, who did not know which chatbot wrote which text, rated ChatGPT's text more complete (4.43 vs 3.86 out of 5) and about equally accurate. A sentiment tool judged ChatGPT's tone neutral and Gemini's negative. Each chatbot answered a single prompt, and no caregivers took part.
custom.studied: palliative care education written by ChatGPT and Gemini for family caregivers of ICU patients

title: Exploring Expectations, Ethical Dimensions, and Values for Voice-Enabled AI Assistants That Support Older Adults and Informal Family Caregivers: Participatory Speculative Design Study

custom.summary: Older adults and family caregivers who imagined future voice assistants for home care saw uses in finding information, prompting care tasks, offering emotional support and linking other devices, the authors report. They also wanted these assistants to be accurate, protective of private data, open about their sources and easy to switch off. Over four months in 2024, 9 people (6 unpaid caregivers of someone aged 65 or older and 3 older adults receiving care) brainstormed, role-played and then critiqued assistant ideas across eight online and in-person workshops. Concerns included invented answers, data breaches, subscription costs and machines displacing human contact, and the authors offer design suggestions such as voice-based access checks and a simple override.
custom.studied: US family caregivers of adults aged 65 or older and older adults receiving family care, imagining voice assistants

title: MEMOR-E: In-Context and Fine-Tuned LLM Personalization for Alzheimer's Assistive Robotics

custom.summary: The authors describe MEMOR-E, a four-legged robot carrying a tablet that offers people with Alzheimer's disease reminders, memory games, photo cues and dialogue, and they report that its language models can produce stage-aware summaries of memory difficulty meant to keep caregivers informed. Classifiers trained on recorded speech from a picture description task (552 transcripts from people with and without Alzheimer's) separated the groups with an AUC of 0.878, a score where 1 means perfect separation. Other tasks scored perfectly, which the authors attribute to healthy speech samples generated by a language model. In a small test, one model role-played nine fictional patients and a second sorted their memory errors by type.
custom.studied: speech transcripts from people with Alzheimer's disease and controls in the DementiaBank Pitt corpus, plus simulated patient personas

title: Development and Evaluation of a Patient-Family Caregiver Dyad mHealth Intervention for Heart Failure Self-Care: Quasi-Experimental Study

custom.summary: In a Korean study of 70 heart failure patients and their family caregivers, the authors report that a 24-week app shared by each pair raised patients' self-care and caregivers' help with it compared with usual care, and improved quality of life for both at six months. The app paired symptom and blood pressure logs that patients could share with caregivers with goal setting, peer groups, nurse calls and a scripted chatbot that sent encouragement, information and reminders three times a week. Gains in knowledge and in the pair's closeness faded within one to three months, and caregiver burden, depression and social support did not change. Groups were enrolled in sequence without randomisation.
custom.studied: Korean adults with heart failure and their family caregivers

title: What do individuals with visual impairment need and want from a dialogue-based digital assistant?

custom.summary: Adults with sight loss and those around them saw value in a conversational digital assistant for tracking down specific facts, but doubted it could offer emotional support, according to this UK study. The authors gathered free-text survey answers from 120 people (87% with visual impairment, about 6% carers or family members, 8% professionals) and held 10 one-to-one interviews. Respondents wanted information on seven topics, including their eye condition, equipment, daily living, sight-loss registration, money and work, emotional support, and help for carers. They described using many sources and running into obstacles reaching them, and the findings are meant to shape the design of future assistants.
custom.studied: UK adults with visual impairment, their carers and family members, and support professionals

title: Improving the lives of ethnically diverse family carers and people living with dementia using digital media resources - Protocol for the Draw-Care randomised controlled trial

custom.summary: The authors describe a three-phase Australian study of Draw-Care, digital resources adapted from the WHO's iSupport Lite messages for family carers of people with dementia from non-English-speaking backgrounds. In the completed first phase, 21 carers, clinicians and service providers, plus three people with dementia, helped shape six animated films and six tip sheets in English and nine other languages. These are hosted on a website with a multilingual virtual 'helper', which 29 carers then tested. The planned second phase is a 12-week waitlist trial with 194 carers measuring caregiver strain on the Zarit Burden Interview, followed by a cost-effectiveness analysis. The paper reports no trial results.
custom.studied: ethnically diverse family carers of people with dementia in Australia

title: Draw-Care, a Co-Designed Multilingual Digital Intervention for Family Carers of People Living With Dementia From Ethnically Diverse Communities: User-Testing Study

custom.summary: Thirty family carers of people with dementia in Australia, most from non-English-speaking backgrounds, found a co-designed website of short animated films and information sheets in 10 languages acceptable and readable, but struggled with three add-on features. Nearly half (14 of 30) needed help to find and use the site's 'helper', a scripted chatbot icon that listed caring situations and pointed to matching films, and its translated name confused some users. The authors report removing the helper and a feedback button, replacing emoji ratings with stars, and correcting translations, such as an outdated, stigmatising Mandarin word for dementia, before a randomised trial.
custom.studied: ethnically diverse Australian family carers of people living with dementia testing a multilingual website

title: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs) for dementia care and research

custom.summary: A small online survey run alongside this review found that people with dementia and their supporters rated seven proposed uses of large language model (LLM) apps as moderately useful to useful. They scored help with navigation, reading and writing highest, and ranked control over their own data as the top priority. The authors surveyed 15 people with dementia and 14 supporters recruited through UK and Australian dementia charities. Five supporters had used tools like ChatGPT, and 8 of the 14 expected a positive overall impact. The review explains how LLMs work, sets out risks such as invented facts, bias and overreliance, and suggests uses including companionship and therapy support.
custom.studied: people with dementia and their supporters in the UK and Australia, alongside literature on LLMs in dementia

sample.of: survey respondents (15 people with dementia, 14 supporters)

title: Information leaflets vs artificial intelligence: comparing perceptions of stroke survivors and professionals in a mixed-methods study

custom.summary: Stroke survivors and family members in this UK study rated ChatGPT-4o answers to common post-stroke questions about as highly as answers from stroke charity websites, while clinicians favoured the charity material and judged it more empathetic. Sixty people (20 clinicians, 20 researchers, 17 survivors and 3 family carers) each rated paired answers without knowing the source. The charity sites covered 13 of the 15 most frequent questions. In interviews, survivors and carers asked for short, plainly worded answers, with a warm tone for health and recovery topics but a more matter-of-fact one for practical support information.
custom.studied: UK stroke survivors, family carers, stroke clinicians and researchers rating ChatGPT-4o and charity website answers

title: Empathy by Design: Aligning Large Language Models for Healthcare Dialogue

custom.summary: The authors report that fine-tuning three small open language models to favour short, warm answers that avoid medical instructions raised their scores for factual consistency, empathy and closeness to reference answers on 500 caregiver-style questions. Training used 1,000 questions drawn from Alzheimer's and caregiving sources. For each, another model wrote a preferred and a rejected answer, and the team applied Direct Preference Optimization, a method that teaches a model which of two answers to favour. For Llama 3.1-8B, an automated correctness score rose from 0.73 to 0.78 and reading level fell from about grade 12.7 to 12.0. All scoring was automated, and no caregivers took part.
custom.studied: open language models fine-tuned to answer caregiver questions about Alzheimer's and dementia care

title: Evaluating the GRACE voice assistant for dementia care among caregivers and healthcare professionals: An interview study

custom.summary: Every participant said they would like to try GRACE, a voice assistant that coaches people with early dementia through spoken exercises based on cognitive stimulation therapy, and the memory exercise drew the most praise. Researchers in Switzerland interviewed 8 healthcare professionals and 5 caregivers in German after they watched a demo video. Participants liked GRACE's friendly opening chat, but felt its corrections made the memory task feel like an exam and called the animal-sound game childish. They expected low digital skills and refusal among people with dementia, and raised privacy and isolation worries. They asked for more personal, open conversation, a caregiver using it alongside at first, and reminders.
custom.studied: healthcare professionals and caregivers of people with dementia in Switzerland and Germany

title: Designing an AI companion to support informal caregivers in role transition: insights from a design science approach

custom.summary: Seven German-speaking family caregivers who tried a GPT-4 chatbot prototype said it sparked brief moments of reflection on their caregiving role, and all found its pointers to support services useful, though none saw it as a substitute for human help. The chatbot asks users whether they see themselves as caregivers, then suggests local services drawn from a resource list curated by the researchers. Participants spoke their thoughts aloud while using it and were then interviewed. From this the authors derived seven design principles, including tailored assessment, clearly sourced information, voice and button input, reflection prompts, and companionship features such as remembering past chats and checking in later.
custom.studied: German-speaking family caregivers trying a GPT-4 chatbot prototype once

title: Large Language Model-Powered Conversational Agent Delivering Problem-Solving Therapy (PST) for Family Caregivers: Enhancing Empathy and Therapeutic Alliance Using In-Context Learning
container-title: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium

custom.summary: The authors report that, among four set-ups of a chatbot built on a large language model (LLM), caregivers rated the two that drew on clinician-chosen example exchanges as the most empathetic and the best at building a working bond. One of those two used a few sample dialogues placed in the prompt. The other used retrieval-augmented generation, meaning the model looks up stored material before it replies. In the study, 28 family caregivers each tried all four versions of the chatbot. It offered problem-solving therapy, a structured talking therapy for working through everyday difficulties, combined with motivational interviewing and behavioral chain analysis. Participants liked that it acknowledged their feelings and gave concrete steps, but the authors note it struggled to balance asking questions with getting to advice.
custom.studied: family caregivers rating four configurations of an LLM chatbot delivering problem-solving therapy

title: Artificial intelligence for educating family caregivers of people with dementia: A mixed methods systematic review

custom.summary: Across 12 studies of AI tools meant to teach family caregivers of people with dementia, the authors report early signs of gains in what caregivers knew, their comfort with digital tools, their emotional well-being and their caring skills, though studies measured different things and found mixed effects. Caregivers generally found the tools usable and worth trying. The tools reviewed ranged from chatbots, virtual assistants and large language model systems to decision-support tools and virtual reality training that reacts to the user. The authors searched nine databases and judged the research base small and weak, with few randomized trials.
custom.studied: studies of AI-based education for family caregivers of people with dementia

title: A Taxonomy of Mental Health and Technology Needs for Alzheimer's and Dementia Caregivers

custom.summary: The authors break dementia caregiver distress into eight separate mental health needs: coping with difficult behaviours, finding support, confidence in one's own ability to cope, family relationships, compassion fatigue, self-care, burnout and emotional balance. They built this list from 52 studies found through a structured literature search and from interviews with 41 US family caregivers, 16 of whom tried a GPT-4o chatbot called Carey. Mapping five kinds of technology against these needs, they report that sensors, reminders and forums serve safety and organisation fairly well. They also report that AI chatbots give round-the-clock advice but show shallow empathy and offer few routes to human help. Family strain, grief and compassion fatigue remain poorly served.
custom.studied: published studies on the mental health of dementia caregivers, plus interviews with US family caregivers of people with dementia

title: Natural language processing-based emotion and usage analysis of an AI-powered chatbot for epilepsy support

custom.summary: Analysing 492 short messages sent to EpiloBot, a Japanese chatbot for epilepsy information and emotional support, the authors report two patterns of use: 332 messages were medical questions, such as how to taper seizure medicines, and 160 were vague or personal queries. The 23 users were 10 people with epilepsy, 10 caregivers and 3 clinicians, over five months in 2024. A language model that scores emotion in text was applied to the five heaviest users. For one of them, messages read as more positive when asking to learn something and less positive when worrying about how others saw them. Because messages were anonymous, caregivers' messages could not be told apart from patients'.
custom.studied: messages sent to an epilepsy support chatbot by people with epilepsy, caregivers and clinicians in Japan

title: Voice Assistants for Mental Health Services: Designing Dialogues with Homebound Older Adults

custom.summary: Participants mostly wanted the voice assistant to speak briefly and plainly. They found emotional lines such as "I'm excited" or "that's a great name" fake or patronizing coming from a machine, but they wanted empathy and encouragement after someone reported low mood or a missed goal. In one-on-one, 90-minute online co-design sessions, 6 homebound older adults with depressive symptoms and 7 family caregivers wrote dialogues for an imagined voice assistant. The assistant would deliver behavioral activation, a depression treatment built around planning rewarding activities. Older adults valued having somewhere to vent without burdening family and wanted to approve each instance of sharing data with caregivers. Caregivers wanted plain statements of how data would be used.
custom.studied: US homebound older adults with depressive symptoms and family caregivers of older adults

title: Evaluating large language models for mild cognitive impairment among older adults: A bilingual comparison of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Kimi

custom.summary: The authors report that ChatGPT-4o, Gemini and Kimi served nonspecialist health workers better than family care partners when answering questions about mild cognitive impairment (MCI, a decline in memory or thinking that falls short of dementia). Care partners got answers that were rated harder to understand and act on. The team put 72 MCI questions to the three chatbots in English and Chinese, and raters scored each answer from 1 to 5 for accuracy, clarity, specificity and how actionable it was. Answers about symptoms and diagnosis scored highest (average 4.11 of 5), and English answers were rated clearer and more specific than Chinese ones.
custom.studied: chatbot answers to MCI questions framed for care partners and for nonspecialist health workers, in English and Chinese

title: Large language models for late-life depression: a blinded benchmark of clinical safety, geriatric appropriateness, and triage

custom.summary: Three consumer chatbots gave clinically acceptable answers to between 60% and 79% of 90 questions about depression in later life, and did worst on the 30 high-risk scenarios (37% to 63%). Psychiatrists who could not see which model wrote each answer rated replies from ChatGPT, Gemini and Doubao against expert standards. Thirty of the questions were worded as a family caregiver would ask them. In an added analysis of those questions, the authors report that the models usually advised emergency help in a crisis but less often told caregivers not to leave the person alone (43% to 79%). Asking the same question twice changed advice in ways that could alter action in 10% to 20% of pairs.
custom.studied: questions about late-life depression written as older adults or their family caregivers would ask them

title: Cultural Prompting Improves the Empathy and Cultural Responsiveness of GPT-Generated Therapy Responses
container-title: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium

custom.summary: The authors report that adding cultural guidance to the prompt made GPT-4o's mental health support replies more culturally fitting and more empathetic for Chinese American family caregivers, while the same change did not significantly improve DeepSeek-V3. In a randomized experiment, 36 participants rated pairs of caregiver messages and model replies, written with and without the cultural prompt, on cultural competence, cultural relevance and perceived empathy. GPT-4o with the cultural prompt was rated highest overall. A mediation analysis, which tests whether one effect works through another, suggested the empathy gain came from the replies being more culturally responsive.
custom.studied: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 therapy-style replies to messages from Chinese American family caregivers

title: MentalChat16K: A Benchmark Dataset for Conversational Mental Health Assistance
container-title: KDD : proceedings. International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining

custom.summary: The authors report that seven open-source language models gave better counseling-style answers after further training (fine-tuning) on MentalChat16K, a released set of about 16,000 question-and-answer pairs for building mental health chatbots. About 6,300 pairs come from 378 transcripts of problem-solving therapy sessions between health coaches and caregivers of people in hospice or palliative care, condensed by a local model and stripped of identifying details. The other 9,775 pairs were written by GPT-3.5. Two AI judges and four human raters scored answers to 200 forum questions, and the AI judges disagreed on whether the synthetic or the caregiver data helped more.
custom.studied: transcripts of coaching sessions with hospice caregivers, plus synthetic counseling conversations

title: AI-Care: A Conversational Agentic System for Task Coordination in Alzheimer's Disease Care

custom.summary: All four pilot users, women with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's or a related dementia aged 84 on average, finished the set tasks by talking with AI-Care, and all said they wanted it added to their existing platform. The authors built this voice-first chatbot on top of I-Care, a remote caregiving platform, so people with dementia can add calendar events, keep to-do lists and check their allergies through conversation. Answers about medicines and allergies are drawn from records that family caregivers check and control, and caregivers can review a log of every change the assistant makes. On 1-to-5 scales, users gave it about 4 for trustworthiness and 4.5 each for competence and likability.
custom.studied: older adults with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's or related dementia using a chatbot on a remote caregiving platform

title: Factors Influencing Adoption of Large Language Models in Health Care: Multicenter Cross-Sectional Mixed Methods Observational Study

custom.summary: The authors report that trust in large language models (LLMs, the AI behind tools such as ChatGPT) was the strongest predictor of willingness to use them, above all among patients and family caregivers, where higher trust raised the odds of willingness about 36-fold. The team surveyed 240 doctors and nurses and 480 patients or caregivers at five hospitals in four Chinese provinces, then interviewed 30 of them. About half of patients and caregivers had heard of LLMs and 26% had used one. Lower education, little use of digital tools and poorer regions went with less willingness, and in interviews patients and caregivers valued plain explanations and conversational help.

title: Cognitive Reablement Using Digital Voice Assistants for People Living With Dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Co-Design Study

custom.summary: The authors report that people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment, their spouses and health professionals jointly shaped an Amazon Alexa program for reablement, meaning support to keep doing daily tasks independently at home. It covers daily living, activities and appointments, and emotional wellbeing. Through online workshops and interviews with 26 people in Australia (9 with dementia or cognitive impairment, 9 spouse care partners, 8 health professionals), medication reminders with self-checking and personalised how-to videos for home appliances were ranked essential. Participants also wanted spoken prompts that start on their own, adjustable volume and speaking speed, setup help, and alerts sent to care partners.

title: Feasibility of a Co-Designed Personalized Cognitive Reablement Program Delivered via Digital Voice Assistants for Older Adults Living With Early-Stage Dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial

custom.summary: In this Australian pilot trial, a program on Amazon Alexa smart displays that helps people keep up daily activities (reablement) proved workable for older adults with early dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Of 35 eligible people, 30 enrolled and 29 finished, and users answered their weekly goal prompts 70% of the time on average. The 15 randomly assigned the program set two or three goals with a psychologist and their care partner, and 9 met or beat them. Usability scores were middling (56 of 100). Apart from more use of memory strategies, the authors found no differences from the control group, including in care partner burden.

title: Large Language Models for Individualized Psychoeducational Tools for Psychosis: A Cross-Sectional Study

custom.summary: Two psychosis experts rated GPT-4's answers to 20 psychosis questions as mostly accurate and clear (averages of 2.88 and 2.93 out of 3) and useful in clinic (4.35 out of 5). Inclusivity scored lower (2.30 out of 3), meaning the answers less often fit people from different cultural and social backgrounds. The answers averaged 330 words at a reading level near grade 15.6, about college level, which the authors say may be too hard for many patients and families. Clinicians at a first-episode psychosis programme wrote the questions to reflect what patients, caregivers and relatives often ask. The authors advise using such tools only with clinician guidance.

title: Attitudes Towards Risks and Benefits of Using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for African American Family Members of a Person with Dementia

custom.summary: In an online survey of 572 US family members of people with dementia or memory problems (470 Black, 102 White), most judged that the benefits of generative AI outweighed its risks across three animated scenarios: AI-written, culturally tailored social work messages, AI scheduling of doctor visits, and AI-enhanced humanoid care robots. Black respondents were about twice as likely as White respondents to view all three favourably (55% against 35%; odds ratio 2.23). Decision-tree models, a machine learning method that sorts people into groups by their traits, singled out family members aged 25 to 34 as the most wary of risks, especially White respondents and those living with the person they care for.

title: Comparing Caregiving Needs in Asian And White Family Caregivers through a Journaling Exercise Delivered by a Conversational Agent

custom.summary: The authors report that Asian American and White family caregivers voiced different needs in three areas: basic physical needs, safety, and self-esteem. Over 14 days, 110 caregivers (26 Asian American, 84 White) wrote about their days in reply to a text-message conversational agent, a chatbot that prompted a daily journal. The team sorted the entries using Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, a framework that ranks human needs from basic survival up to esteem and personal growth. They conclude that caregivers from different cultural and ethnic backgrounds need support and resources suited to their culture.

title: Assessing the Role of the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) in Alzheimer's Disease Management: Comparative Study of Neurologist- and Artificial Intelligence-Generated Responses

custom.summary: Neurologists who did not know the source of each answer rated ChatGPT's replies to common Alzheimer's disease questions above replies written by neurologists (overall 4.4 vs 3.9 on a 5-point scale). Five family caregivers rated both sources the same (3.9). The authors put 14 questions on diagnosis, treatment and daily care to two ChatGPT versions, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, in English and in Chinese, and had four neurologists answer the same questions, giving 112 responses. Five neurologists and five caregivers then scored them. The authors report no significant gap between the two model versions, and the neurologist raters found the English answers easier to follow than the Chinese ones.

title: ADRD-Bench: A Preliminary LLM Benchmark for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias

custom.summary: Across 36 large language models, the authors report accuracy from 0.58 to 0.96 on 149 new true/false and multiple-choice questions about daily dementia caregiving, with gpt-5.5 scoring highest; models tuned for medicine showed no clear edge over general ones on these. The caregiving questions were built from the Aging Brain Care program's caregiver education handouts and checked by a senior clinician. They sit beside 1,438 dementia items gathered from seven existing medical benchmarks. In worked examples, even top models overgeneralized across disease stages, or treated a person looking away during conversation as a problem to fix when it often signals overload.
custom.studied: 36 large language models answering dementia clinical and caregiving questions

title: MemoryCompanion: A Smart Healthcare Solution to Empower Efficient Alzheimer's Care Via Unleashing Generative AI

custom.summary: The authors report that MemoryCompanion answered accurately about a person's name, family and home, replied warmly to grief and loneliness, and gently corrected a false memory, though casual chat sometimes fell short of sounding human. The system, built for people with Alzheimer's disease, gives GPT-3.5 Turbo a profile of each person and speaks through a cloned voice and animated face of a familiar loved one. Its stated aims are to ease isolation and lighten the load on family carers. It was tested on 100 synthetic patient profiles, drawn from 10,000 that GPT-4 wrote; each was asked nine questions, and answers were scored from 1 to 5.
custom.studied: a voice and talking-face GPT companion for people with Alzheimer's disease, tested on synthetic patient profiles

title: InterMind: Doctor-Patient-Family Interactive Depression Assessment Empowered by Large Language Models

custom.summary: The authors report that a depression assessment model fed both patient and family accounts outperformed versions using either one alone, reaching an F1 score (a combined accuracy measure) of 0.862 on one Chinese clinical interview dataset against 0.762 for patient-only input. InterMind pairs a chatbot that talks separately with a patient and family members with a second model that drafts a structured diagnostic report and gives care advice to the family. Family conversations were simulated by GPT-4 from existing patient data, with 809 test subjects across three datasets. Five psychiatrists judged reports for 129 subjects, and 18 volunteers preferred the chatbot to GPT-4 on engagement and overall quality.
custom.studied: an LLM depression assessment system that converses with patients and their family members, tested on simulated family dialogues

title: Empowering Informal Caregivers of Persons With Early-Stage Dementia by Large Language Models: Mixed Methods Evaluation

custom.summary: Dementia care experts rated answers from a version of ChatGPT-4o given caregiving-specific instructions as more useful, more relevant and more satisfying than answers from standard ChatGPT-4o, the authors report. Most other ratings did not differ. The team wrote these instructions (prompt engineering, meaning carefully worded guidance given to the model) using 90 expert-written question-and-answer pairs on dementia knowledge, cultural values, social support and coping. They then put 32 typical caregiver questions to both versions. Twelve raters, mostly nurses and physicians with only a few family caregivers, scored the 64 answers blind on a 7-point scale and were then interviewed. In those interviews, raters described both versions as wordy.
custom.studied: ChatGPT-4o answers to questions typical of caregivers of people with early-stage dementia, rated by dementia care experts
